difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that antibiotic resistance is a serious problem; disagreement is on a specific axis (whether overprescription by physicians is the primary driver), requiring the test-taker to isolate the real point of contention from shared premises.
stimulus: Dr. Fenn: The alarming rise in antibiotic-resistant bacteria is driven primarily by physicians overprescribing antibiotics for viral infections. If we restrict prescriptions more aggressively, resistance rates will begin to fall. Dr. Osei: You are focusing on the wrong culprit. Agricultural overuse of antibiotics — feeding livestock subtherapeutic doses to accelerate growth — releases far greater quantities of antibiotics into the environment than overprescription does. Restricting physician prescriptions alone will accomplish little.
questionStem: Dr. Fenn and Dr. Osei disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: antibiotic resistance poses a serious threat to public health

choices.label: B
choices.text: agricultural antibiotic use contributes to antibiotic resistance

choices.label: C
choices.text: physician overprescription is the principal cause of rising antibiotic resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: restricting antibiotic prescriptions would have any effect on resistance rates

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments have an obligation to regulate antibiotic use in livestock farming

explanations.correct: Dr. Fenn explicitly identifies physician overprescription as the primary driver; Dr. Osei explicitly identifies agricultural use as the greater source and says physician overprescription is not the main culprit. Both speakers directly address and take opposing positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat resistance as a serious problem; neither disputes this.
explanations.B: One-sided — Dr. Osei asserts agricultural use contributes; Dr. Fenn does not deny that agricultural use contributes, only that physician overprescription is the bigger factor.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the precise axis of disagreement.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — Dr. Osei says restricting prescriptions 'alone' will accomplish little, not that it will have zero effect. Dr. Fenn says it will cause resistance to fall. The nuance in Dr. Osei's 'alone' makes this a near-miss trap, not the clearest point of issue.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses governmental regulatory obligations.

difficultyReason: Both speakers support some form of carbon taxation; the disagreement is about revenue allocation, a specific sub-issue that test-takers may overlook in favor of the superficially broader agreement on carbon taxes.
stimulus: Moreno: A carbon tax is the most efficient tool we have for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Revenue from the tax should be returned directly to citizens as dividends, ensuring that lower-income households are not disproportionately burdened. Peña: I agree that a carbon tax is the right approach. However, returning revenue as citizen dividends squanders an opportunity. That revenue should be invested in green infrastructure — renewable energy grids and public transit — which will reduce emissions far more effectively over the long term.
questionStem: Moreno and Peña disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: a carbon tax is an efficient mechanism for reducing greenhouse gas emissions

choices.label: B
choices.text: lower-income households are disproportionately affected by carbon pricing

choices.label: C
choices.text: green infrastructure investment would reduce emissions over the long term

choices.label: D
choices.text: carbon tax revenue should be distributed to citizens rather than invested in infrastructure

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments are capable of administering a carbon tax effectively

explanations.correct: Moreno explicitly advocates returning revenue as citizen dividends; Peña explicitly argues that revenue should fund green infrastructure instead. Both speakers directly address and take opposing stances on this allocation question.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers explicitly agree that a carbon tax is the right approach.
explanations.B: One-sided — Moreno raises this concern as a reason for dividends; Peña does not address whether lower-income households are disproportionately burdened.
explanations.C: One-sided — Peña asserts this; Moreno does not address the long-term emission impact of infrastructure investment.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker discusses governmental capacity to administer the tax.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that social media affects adolescent mental health; they differ on whether the relationship is primarily causal or correlational, a conceptually nuanced distinction that generates plausible wrong answers.
stimulus: Aldridge: Research consistently shows that heavy social media use causes depression and anxiety in teenagers. The mechanism is clear: constant social comparison and cyberbullying directly harm developing self-esteem. Platforms should be required to implement use-limiting features for minors. Burak: The data do not support that conclusion. Studies showing a correlation between social media use and poor mental health cannot establish causation — teenagers who are already struggling with depression may simply be more likely to spend time online. Mandatory use restrictions are premature.
questionStem: Aldridge and Burak disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: teenagers who use social media heavily are more likely to report symptoms of depression

choices.label: B
choices.text: social media platforms have any responsibility for the well-being of their users

choices.label: C
choices.text: social comparison is a feature of adolescent social interaction generally

choices.label: D
choices.text: social media use is a cause, rather than merely a correlate, of depression in adolescents

choices.label: E
choices.text: legislators should be permitted to regulate the design features of social media platforms

explanations.correct: Aldridge asserts a clear causal mechanism; Burak directly disputes causation by arguing that correlational studies cannot establish it and that the relationship may be reversed. Both speakers explicitly take opposing positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Aldridge's argument presupposes this correlation, and Burak explicitly references studies showing it; neither disputes the correlation itself.
explanations.B: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses platform responsibility in general terms.
explanations.C: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses adolescent social comparison beyond the social media context.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — both mention mandatory restrictions, but neither addresses the broader constitutional or legal question of legislative authority to regulate platform design.

difficultyReason: Both speakers value judicial independence; their disagreement targets a specific institutional design question. One trap answer is an agreement; another is one-sided.
stimulus: Laird: Judicial elections undermine the independence of the courts. When judges must campaign for votes, they inevitably tailor their rulings to please the electorate rather than faithfully applying the law. Appointment by a merit-selection commission is the only way to preserve impartiality. Kim: Judicial elections are not the problem you describe. Accountability to the public is itself a democratic value, and elected judges are no less faithful to the law than appointed ones. Insulating judges entirely from democratic input creates its own risks of unresponsive, elitist jurisprudence.
questionStem: Laird and Kim disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: judicial impartiality is an important value in a legal system

choices.label: B
choices.text: judicial elections compromise the impartiality of judges

choices.label: C
choices.text: merit-selection commissions produce judges who are more qualified than elected judges

choices.label: D
choices.text: democratic accountability is a legitimate concern in the design of judicial systems

choices.label: E
choices.text: judges appointed by commissions have longer terms than elected judges

explanations.correct: Laird explicitly argues that elections force judges to tailor rulings to voters, compromising impartiality; Kim explicitly denies this, arguing that elected judges are no less faithful to the law. Both take clear opposing positions.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat impartiality as important; Laird defends it by opposing elections, and Kim invokes it implicitly by denying elections undermine it.
explanations.C: One-sided — Laird does not argue that commission-appointed judges are more qualified, only more impartial; Kim does not address qualifications.
explanations.D: Agreement in disguise — Laird does not deny that democratic accountability is a legitimate value; Kim explicitly invokes it. Laird's preference for commissions is about a different concern.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker discusses term lengths.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the rainforest has ecological value; disagreement is specifically about whether sustainable logging can preserve that value, a nuanced axis surrounded by apparent common ground.
stimulus: Nkosi: Sustainable logging practices allow us to harvest timber commercially while preserving the ecological integrity of rainforests. Certification programs that enforce strict harvest limits and reforestation requirements have proven effective. Rainforests managed under such programs retain their biodiversity. Vega: That is wishful thinking. No logging operation, however carefully managed, can replicate the ecological complexity of an old-growth forest. Once primary forest is disturbed, the biodiversity losses are effectively permanent on any human timescale. True ecological preservation requires leaving these forests entirely untouched.
questionStem: Nkosi and Vega disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: rainforest biodiversity has significant ecological value

choices.label: B
choices.text: certification programs for sustainable logging have been implemented in some regions

choices.label: C
choices.text: commercial logging operations generate economic benefits for local communities

choices.label: D
choices.text: sustainably managed logging can preserve the biodiversity of rainforests

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments have an obligation to protect old-growth forests from commercial development

explanations.correct: Nkosi explicitly asserts that certified sustainable logging preserves biodiversity; Vega explicitly denies that any managed logging can replicate or preserve old-growth ecological complexity. Both speakers directly address and oppose each other on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat rainforest biodiversity as valuable; their dispute is about whether sustainable logging threatens it.
explanations.B: One-sided — Nkosi references the existence of certification programs; Vega does not address whether such programs exist, only whether they succeed.
explanations.C: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses economic benefits to local communities.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker discusses governmental obligations specifically.

difficultyReason: Both speakers acknowledge that Renaissance art reflects its historical context; the disagreement concerns whether biographical knowledge of the artist is necessary for full aesthetic appreciation — a nuanced interpretive claim that creates plausible traps.
stimulus: Chandra: To fully appreciate a Renaissance painting, one must understand the biographical context of the artist — the patron relationships, personal hardships, and theological commitments that shaped each work. Without that knowledge, a viewer grasps only the surface. Torres: I disagree. A great painting communicates its meanings visually, through composition, color, and form. Viewers who know nothing of an artist's biography regularly have profound aesthetic experiences before such works. Biographical context may enrich appreciation, but it is not necessary for it.
questionStem: Chandra and Torres disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: Renaissance paintings reflect the theological beliefs of the era in which they were created

choices.label: B
choices.text: biographical knowledge of an artist can enhance a viewer's appreciation of the artist's work

choices.label: C
choices.text: an understanding of artistic composition is relevant to aesthetic appreciation

choices.label: D
choices.text: knowledge of an artist's biography is necessary for a full appreciation of that artist's painting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renaissance patrons exerted significant influence over the content of commissioned artworks

explanations.correct: Chandra says biographical context is necessary for full appreciation; Torres explicitly denies necessity while conceding biographical context may enrich appreciation. Both speakers directly address whether biographical knowledge is necessary.
explanations.A: One-sided — Chandra references theological commitments; Torres does not address whether Renaissance paintings reflect theological beliefs.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Torres concedes biographical context 'may enrich appreciation'; Chandra clearly agrees. Neither disputes that it can enhance appreciation — only whether it is required.
explanations.C: One-sided — Torres references composition, color, and form; Chandra does not address whether composition knowledge is relevant.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses patron influence on content in general terms.

difficultyReason: Both speakers support universal basic income in principle; their disagreement targets work incentives specifically, creating a clear but narrow axis that test-takers may miss when distracted by the broader shared premise.
stimulus: Reyes: A universal basic income — a guaranteed monthly payment to every citizen regardless of employment status — would eliminate the poverty trap created by means-tested benefits and give workers the bargaining power to refuse exploitative jobs. Critics worry it will discourage work, but people have intrinsic motivations to contribute; the evidence from pilot programs shows employment levels remain stable. Hartmann: The pilot program evidence is too limited to be reassuring. When a program is universal and permanent rather than temporary and localized, the incentive effects are amplified. A guaranteed income with no work requirement will meaningfully reduce labor force participation over time.
questionStem: Reyes and Hartmann disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: means-tested benefit programs create disincentives that trap recipients in poverty

choices.label: B
choices.text: a universal basic income would reduce the bargaining power of low-wage workers

choices.label: C
choices.text: pilot programs studying universal basic income have been conducted

choices.label: D
choices.text: a permanent universal basic income would significantly reduce labor force participation

choices.label: E
choices.text: citizens in a wealthy society have a right to a guaranteed minimum income

explanations.correct: Reyes argues that evidence shows employment levels remain stable and that intrinsic motivation preserves labor force participation; Hartmann argues that a permanent, universal program would meaningfully reduce labor force participation. Both speakers directly address and take opposing positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: One-sided — Reyes asserts means-tested programs create poverty traps; Hartmann does not address this claim.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Reyes argues UBI increases workers' bargaining power; neither speaker discusses a reduction in bargaining power.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — both speakers acknowledge pilot programs exist; Hartmann's criticism is about the adequacy of such evidence, not whether programs occurred.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses rights-based arguments for guaranteed income.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that indigenous languages are disappearing; they disagree specifically about whether formal schooling in those languages is effective at reversing decline — a targeted claim requiring careful reading of each speaker's position.
stimulus: Wolfe: The most effective way to revitalize an endangered indigenous language is to integrate it into formal schooling. When children are immersed in a language through structured instruction from an early age, they achieve genuine fluency rather than mere familiarity. Immersion schools have demonstrably reversed language decline in several communities. Clearwater: Formal schooling alone cannot save a language. Language vitality depends on its use in everyday community life — in markets, ceremonies, and homes. When a language is spoken only in classrooms, children learn it as an academic subject rather than as a living means of communication, and it continues to decline outside school walls.
questionStem: Wolfe and Clearwater disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: indigenous languages are disappearing at an alarming rate

choices.label: B
choices.text: children who attend immersion schools achieve some degree of fluency in the target language

choices.label: C
choices.text: the use of a language in daily community life contributes to its vitality

choices.label: D
choices.text: formal schooling is sufficient on its own to reverse the decline of an endangered language

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments should fund immersion school programs for speakers of endangered languages

explanations.correct: Wolfe argues that immersion schooling has demonstrably reversed language decline, implying formal schooling is an effective and sufficient tool; Clearwater explicitly argues that formal schooling alone cannot save a language. Both speakers address and oppose each other on the sufficiency of formal schooling.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat language decline as a real problem they wish to address; neither disputes that languages are disappearing.
explanations.B: One-sided — Wolfe asserts immersion produces fluency; Clearwater does not dispute that children learn the language in school, only that school-based learning is insufficient for vitality.
explanations.C: One-sided — Clearwater asserts this; Wolfe does not deny that community use matters, only that formal schooling is effective.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses governmental funding obligations.

difficultyReason: Both speakers value historical accuracy; disagreement targets whether presentism in historical judgment is appropriate, a nuanced normative claim that generates near-miss traps about shared values.
stimulus: Okafor: Historians should evaluate historical figures by the moral standards of their own time, not ours. Judging a seventeenth-century slaveholder by twenty-first-century norms is anachronistic — it distorts our understanding of the past and imposes a false moral clarity on genuinely complex historical situations. Svensson: That approach conveniently excuses atrocities. The wrongness of enslaving another person does not depend on when in history it occurred. If we restrict moral judgment to the standards contemporaries applied, we lose the ability to say that any historical injustice was truly wrong, and history becomes a chronicle without moral meaning.
questionStem: Okafor and Svensson disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: slavery was widely practiced and economically significant in the seventeenth century

choices.label: B
choices.text: historians have an obligation to understand historical figures in their own context

choices.label: C
choices.text: applying contemporary moral standards to historical figures distorts historical understanding

choices.label: D
choices.text: some actions are morally wrong regardless of the era in which they were committed

choices.label: E
choices.text: moral standards have changed significantly between the seventeenth and twenty-first centuries

explanations.correct: Okafor explicitly argues that judging past figures by present standards distorts our understanding of history; Svensson explicitly rejects this, arguing instead that restricting judgment to contemporary standards loses moral meaning. Both speakers directly address and oppose each other on whether applying modern standards distorts historical understanding.
explanations.A: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the economic or demographic dimensions of seventeenth-century slavery.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Okafor explicitly endorses understanding figures in their own context, and Svensson does not deny that contextual understanding is valuable, only that it should substitute for moral judgment.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — Svensson implies this, and Okafor's view suggests standards are era-relative, but Okafor's argument is about historical methodology, not a direct denial of universal moral truths. This is a near-miss that focuses on the underlying metaphysical claim rather than the methodological disagreement both speakers address.
explanations.E: One-sided — Okafor's argument presupposes standards differ across eras; Svensson does not address whether standards have changed, only that change in standards does not affect the wrongness of certain acts.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree open-source software has benefits; their disagreement focuses on whether it produces more secure software than proprietary alternatives — a specific technical claim with plausible agreement traps on both sides.
stimulus: Drayton: Open-source software is more secure than proprietary software. Because the source code is publicly available, a global community of developers can identify and patch vulnerabilities far more quickly than any single company's internal team. The sheer number of independent reviewers means that bugs are shallow — quickly found and fixed. Lim: That logic is flawed. Having source code publicly available means that malicious actors can study it just as easily as defenders can. Many open-source projects are maintained by tiny volunteer teams with no resources for systematic security auditing. Proprietary software teams, by contrast, can dedicate full-time security professionals to the task.
questionStem: Drayton and Lim disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: open-source software projects are sometimes maintained by small volunteer teams

choices.label: B
choices.text: the public availability of source code provides any advantage in identifying software vulnerabilities

choices.label: C
choices.text: proprietary software development companies employ professional security teams

choices.label: D
choices.text: open-source software is, on balance, more secure than proprietary software

choices.label: E
choices.text: software security is an important consideration for both individual users and organizations

explanations.correct: Drayton explicitly argues that open-source software is more secure due to community review; Lim explicitly argues that public code availability aids attackers as much as defenders and that proprietary teams are better resourced — directly contesting the superiority claim. Both speakers address and oppose each other on the overall security comparison.
explanations.A: One-sided — Lim asserts this; Drayton does not address team size or resources.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Drayton argues public availability is an advantage; Lim argues it is a double-edged sword. This is close, but Lim's claim is not that public code provides no advantage for defenders, only that it equally benefits attackers, making the net effect negative. The cleaner disagreement is the overall comparative security claim in D.
explanations.C: One-sided — Lim references proprietary security professionals; Drayton does not address proprietary team structures.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses whether security matters to users generally; both presuppose it does.
